summary: Defines a way to check that an MPLS label switched path really works in the data plane. A probe called an MPLS echo request travels along the path and an echo reply reports the result, helping find failures that normal ping may miss.

eli5.summary: Like sending a marked boat down a river to check it flows all the way, this sends a test message along a path and gets back a note about what happened.

subtitle: A ping and traceroute for MPLS label switched paths that follows the same route as real traffic.

tldr.problem: An MPLS label switched path can silently drop or misroute user traffic without the control plane noticing, and operators need a way to detect these black holes and find where they are.
tldr.mechanism: A router sends an MPLS echo request, a UDP packet that names the path being tested, along the same data path as ordinary traffic. The router at the end of the path (ping) or each router along it (traceroute) checks the claim against its own state and returns an MPLS echo reply with a return code.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8029 consolidates and replaces RFCs 4379, 6424, 6829 and 7537 into one LSP ping specification. It is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by three later RFCs.

today: RFC 8029 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2017. It obsoletes RFC 4379, RFC 6424, RFC 6829 and RFC 7537, and is updated by RFC 8611, RFC 9041 and RFC 9570.

sections.title: What LSP Ping Is For
sections.content:
RFC 8029 describes a simple and efficient mechanism to detect data-plane failures in MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs). It defines a probe called an MPLS echo request and a response called an MPLS echo reply.

The key design point is that echo requests follow the same data path that normal MPLS packets of that path would take. They validate the data plane first, and secondarily check it against the control plane. Checking the control plane by itself is valuable but not covered here.

The document is a cleanup and consolidation. It incorporates outstanding errata, replaces EXP with Traffic Class, adds pseudowire FECs advertised over IPv6, adds the IPv6 Router Alert option for MPLS OAM, deprecates the Downstream Mapping TLV in favour of the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV, and obsoletes RFCs 4379, 6424, 6829 and 7537. It also updates RFC 1122, because of its special use of the 127/8 address range.
sections.eli5: This is a rulebook for a tool that tests a route through a network. The test message travels the same road as real traffic, so if the road is broken the test finds out.

sections.title: Motivation and Design Choices
sections.content:
When an LSP fails to deliver user traffic, the MPLS control plane cannot always detect it. The RFC wants a tool to find such traffic black holes or misrouting within a reasonable time, and to isolate the fault. It is modeled on ping and traceroute: ping mode checks end-to-end connectivity, and traceroute mode checks hop by hop.

The basic idea is to verify that packets of a given Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) really end their MPLS path on a router that is an egress for that FEC. In ping mode the packet reaches the control plane of the egress router, which checks this. In traceroute mode each transit router checks that it belongs on the path and returns extra information so the control plane can be compared with what is actually forwarded.

Echo requests are routed by their label stack alone, never by IP destination address. To keep a stray diagnostic packet from reaching a customer, the destination is a random IPv4 address from 127/8 (or the matching range inside an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address). Hosts discard such packets by default, and RFC 1812 tells routers not to forward them. The range also offers about 16M addresses to vary, which helps exercise Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) paths. The packets also carry the Router Alert option so transit routers look at them.

One suggested use is to ping a FEC periodically and, if the ping fails, run a traceroute to find the fault. Running traceroute regularly puts more load on transit routers and should be used with caution.
sections.eli5: The test message is addressed to a place that ordinary computers throw away, so it cannot wander off to a real customer. It is steered only by the path labels, so it takes the real route.

sections.title: The Echo Request and Reply Packet
sections.content:
An MPLS echo request or reply is a possibly labeled IPv4 or IPv6 UDP packet. Its payload starts with fixed fields, followed by a list of TLVs (Type-Length-Value items).

  • Version Number: currently 1.
  • Global Flags: three flags are defined. V asks the receiver to validate the FEC stack, T (respond only if TTL expired) tells a receiver to drop the request and not answer when the incoming label TTL is more than 1, and R asks for reverse-path FEC information.
  • Message Type: 1 for an echo request, 2 for an echo reply.
  • Reply Mode: 1 do not reply, 2 reply by UDP, 3 reply by UDP with Router Alert, 4 reply through an application-level control channel.
  • Return Code and Return Subcode: the result, set to zero by the sender.
  • Sender's Handle and Sequence Number: chosen by the sender and used to match replies to requests.
  • Two 64-bit NTP-format timestamps: when the request was sent and when it was received.

Reply Mode 1 can be used for one-way connectivity tests, where the receiver may log gaps in sequence numbers or keep delay and jitter statistics. Mode 3 helps when the normal IP return path is deemed unreliable, but all intermediate routers must then know how to forward echo replies.
sections.eli5: Every test message starts with a small form: what kind of message it is, a ticket number, the time it was sent, and how to send the answer back.

sections.title: TLVs and the Target FEC Stack
sections.content:
Each TLV has a 16-bit type, a 16-bit length counted in octets, and a value that is zero padded to a 4-octet boundary. TLVs can nest; nested ones are called sub-TLVs. Types below 32768 are mandatory: an implementation must support them or answer with Return Code 2. Types of 32768 and above are optional and should be ignored if not understood.

The central TLV is the Target FEC Stack, which every echo request MUST carry. It is a list of sub-TLVs identifying the path being tested, with the first element matching the top of the label stack. The RFC defines sub-types for LDP IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes, RSVP IPv4 and IPv6 LSPs, VPN IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes, L2 VPN endpoints, FEC 128 and FEC 129 pseudowires, BGP labeled prefixes, generic prefixes, and a Nil FEC.

Other TLVs include the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV (type 20), which asks each router to describe its downstream interfaces, labels and ECMP multipath information; the Pad TLV, used to make a message of a specific size; the Vendor Enterprise Number; the Interface and Label Stack TLV, which reports where the request arrived and with what labels; Errored TLVs, which list mandatory TLVs that were not understood; and the Reply TOS Octet TLV.

Example from the RFC: to check that label 1001 reaches the egress that announced 192.0.2.1 through LDP, send an echo request with one LDP IPv4 prefix FEC, prefix 192.0.2.1/32, using label 1001.
sections.eli5: After the form come labeled pockets of extra information. The most important pocket says which route is being tested, like writing the destination address on a parcel.

sections.title: Return Codes
sections.content:
The echo reply reports its verdict in the Return Code, with the Return Subcode giving the label stack depth for codes that need one. The bottom of the stack counts as depth 1, and a depth of 0 means no value specified.

The main codes are 3 (the replying router is an egress for the FEC), 8 (label switched at this depth, the normal answer from a transit router), 4 (no mapping for the FEC), 10 (the mapping for this FEC is not the given label) and 11 (no label entry). Code 1 means the echo request was malformed, 2 means one or more TLVs were not understood, and 14 tells the sender to read the codes inside the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV, which is used when a node has several downstream paths.

Codes 5 and 6 report a Downstream Mapping mismatch and an unknown upstream interface index. Code 9 means the label was switched but the outgoing interface has no MPLS forwarding, 13 means the ping ended early because the label stack shrank to a single label, and 15 means label switched with a FEC change.
sections.eli5: The answer comes back with a number, like a report card. One number means you reached the end, another means a signpost is missing, and another means the signpost points the wrong way.

sections.title: How Requests and Replies Are Handled
sections.content:
Sending. The request is a UDP packet from a routable sender address to a destination in 127/8, with IP TTL 1 and the Router Alert option set. Its destination UDP port is 3503, assigned by IANA, and the sender picks the source port. In ping mode the outermost label TTL is set to 255. In traceroute mode it starts at 1 and goes up one hop at a time, and the request SHOULD include a Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV.

Receiving. A router hands the packet to its control plane through a processing exception such as the Router Alert option, TTL expiry or a 127/8 destination, then recognises it by UDP port 3503. It checks the packet is well formed, then walks the label stack, looking up each label. A pop-and-continue label is skipped. A swap or pop-and-switch label is a transit hop. If no labels remain, the router acts as the egress and validates the FEC against its own label mapping.

Replying. The reply is a UDP packet with IP TTL 255, sent to the source address and port of the request. It copies the Sender's Handle, Sequence Number and sent timestamp, and fills in the received timestamp. The sender matches replies using the destination UDP port and the Sender's Handle, then checks the Sequence Number, and for traceroute copies the returned Downstream Detailed Mappings into its next request with the TTL raised by one.

Special cases.

  • With ECMP, the ingress uses the multipath information returned by traceroute to craft requests that exercise each path, though full coverage may not be possible.
  • When a path enters a tunnel or a stitched LSP, transit nodes can report FEC stack changes. They may use the Nil FEC to hide tunnel details.
  • If a router does not support LSP ping, no reply comes back, so traceroute continues with higher TTLs.
sections.eli5: For a ping, the message goes all the way and the last stop answers. For a traceroute, the message is allowed one more stop each time, so every stop on the road answers in turn and you can see where it breaks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the security needs of LSP ping are similar to those of ICMP ping. It names three kinds of attack: denial of service by flooding routers with echo traffic, tampering with or spoofing requests and replies to hide the true state of the data plane, and unauthorized use of LSP ping to learn about the network.

Implementations are RECOMMENDED to rate-limit LSP ping traffic going to the control plane on the well-known UDP port, and to check the source addresses of requests against an access list. Spoofed replies are unlikely to work because they must match an outstanding Sender's Handle and Sequence Number, and an implementation MAY also require the sent timestamp to match exactly. Operators can add border filtering inside an administrative domain.

The rest of the Pad TLV is ignored on receipt and so could serve as a clandestine channel. The special use of 127/8 applies only with UDP port 3503, and a router receiving a 127/8 packet to any other port treats it as a martian under RFC 1812.
sections.eli5: Since anyone could shout test messages at a router, the router should limit how many it answers and only answer people on its list.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Lineage
sections.content:
IANA allocated TCP and UDP port 3503 for LSP echo requests and replies, and maintains a set of MPLS LSP Ping registries for message types, reply modes, return codes, TLVs, flags and several address and pad types. In the 0-255 registries, values 0-191 are assigned by Standards Action, 192-251 need a specification, and 252-255 are for vendor private use. Vendor private values require a Vendor Enterprise Number TLV in the message.

The text also records the lineage of the document: it folds in RFC 6424, RFC 6829 and RFC 7537, and replaces RFC 4379, the original LSP ping specification.
sections.eli5: A central office hands out the official numbers so that different companies do not use the same code for different things.
